scope: What the IECEP is in law, which ethical duties bind a registered electronics professional, and how a complaint against one is heard and punished.
intuition: The Code of Ethics is not a courtesy: RA 9292 makes the Board adopt it and makes its violation a ground for suspension or revocation and, at the outer edge, a criminal offence.
concept: **What the IECEP is, in law.** The Integrated Electronics Engineering Professionals of the Philippines is the profession's **one integrated and accredited professional organization** under RA 9292 §32: a single national organization of PECEs, ECEs and ECTs, registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a non-stock, non-profit corporation and recognised by the Board, the Commission and all government agencies as the one and only integrated and accredited national organization for those professionals. Two consequences follow that exam questions use. First, **every** PECE, ECE and ECT, upon registration with the Commission, **ipso facto becomes a member** of the accredited professional organization — membership is not an optional affiliation. Second, the APO is charged with implementing the continuing professional education and/or development programme, and with accrediting other organizations or entities to provide CPE/CPD; compliance is one of the requisites for maintaining membership in good standing. Members in good standing are issued an **annual membership card** indicating the membership number and validity period, and that card must be affixed to all plans, specifications and any document signed by the member in the course of practice; failure to maintain good standing is a cause for listing the individual as **delinquent** in the Board's roster under §25. Membership in the IECEP does not bar membership in other associations of the electronics engineering and electronics technician professions (§32).

**Where the Code of Ethics comes from and what it binds.** RA 9292 §30 provides that the Board shall adopt a **Code of Ethics and a Code of Technical Standards of Practice** for electronics engineers and electronics technicians, **which shall be promulgated by the accredited professional organization**. RA 9292 §7 gives the Board the power to “adopt and administer” the Code of Ethics and the Code of Technical Standards of Practice, and §39 lists them among the instruments the Board adopts and promulgates, subject to Commission approval, in coordination with the APO. Their reach is explicit: the certificate of registration and the PIC are not merely an examination credential but a licence to practise the electronics engineering profession with all the privileges appurtenant, subject to compliance with all applicable requirements (§19) — and one of those requirements is conduct consistent with the Code. The Code is enforced by three separate mechanisms, and knowing which one a question is testing is most of the work: an **administrative** mechanism before the Board, a **licensure** mechanism in the renewal and roster rules, and a **criminal** mechanism under the penal provision.

**The fundamental canons.** The accredited professional organization's code, adopted by the Board, is built on the canons that govern professional engineering practice in the Philippines. In substance, and in the form the board exam tests them: **public safety and welfare are paramount** — the engineer holds the safety, health and welfare of the public foremost and must not approve or seal work that endangers life or property; **competence and honesty in qualifications** — the professional undertakes only work for which he is qualified by training and experience, does not misrepresent his competence, and does not lend his name, seal or signature to work not prepared by him or under his direct supervision; **objectivity and truthfulness** — reports, findings, specifications and test results must be objective and truthful, and only what was actually done may be certified; **confidentiality** — information obtained in the course of professional employment is not disclosed without consent except where required by law or where disclosure is necessary to protect the public; **conflict of interest and integrity** — no undisclosed financial or other interest that could compromise judgment, and no acceptance of compensation from more than one party for the same service without the knowledge and consent of all concerned; **fidelity to clients and employers** — services rendered faithfully, no competing or conflicting employment accepted without disclosure, and a duty to advise the client or employer when a project is not viable or is unsafe; **professional conduct and lawful practice** — no practice outside the scope of one's registration, no aiding of unlicensed practice, no fraud or deceit in obtaining or using a certificate, PIC or seal; **fair dealing with colleagues** — no false or malicious criticism of another's work, and credit given where due; and **limits on advertising and solicitation** — the professional may advertise his services only in a manner that is truthful, not misleading, dignified and free from self-laudation, and may not solicit or compete for work by improper means such as underbidding through reduction in the quality of service or offering commissions. Two RA 9292 provisions give these canons concrete teeth: §28 makes the practice of electronics engineering and electronics technician a **professional service, admission to which is determined on the basis of the individual's personal qualifications**, so that no firm, company, partnership, association or corporation may be registered or licensed as such for the practice, although registrants may form partnerships, associations or corporations among themselves or with allied professionals and render services collectively — with the proviso that **individual members are responsible for their own respective acts**; and §35 makes it an offence for a PECE to sign or seal plans, technical descriptions or other documents prepared by or under the supervision of **another** PECE unless the document clearly indicates the part of the work actually performed by the former, and for any person other than the PECE or ECE in charge to sign for electronics engineering work not actually performed by him.

**Who hears a complaint, and what it costs.** A violation of the Code of Ethics is the Board's business. RA 9292 §7 gives the Board power to hear and decide violations of the Act, its implementing rules and regulations, the **Code of Ethics** and the Code of Technical Standards of Practice, with authority to issue subpoena ad testificandum and subpoena duces tecum to secure the attendance of witnesses and the production of documents; hearings on cases that strictly concern the practice of the profession must be presided over by at least one (1) member of the Board, assisted by a Legal or Hearing Officer of the Commission, while purely administrative cases may be delegated to authorised officers of the Commission. Board resolutions, orders and decisions in administrative cases are appealable to the Commission within **fifteen (15) days** from receipt; the Commission may affirm, reverse, dismiss, deny the appeal or remand, and if no appeal is taken the decision becomes final and immediately enforceable. RA 8981 §9 confirms the board's jurisdiction over violations of its own law, rules and Code of Ethics, its subpoena power, the delegation rule, and the 15-day finality of an unappealed decision. The sanctions run in this order: the Board may, **upon proper notice and hearing**, revoke or suspend the validity of the certificate of registration and the corresponding PIC, or cancel a special permit, for unprofessional or unethical conduct, malpractice, incompetence, any violation of the Act, the IRR, the Code of Ethics or the Code of Technical Standards of Practice, or where fraud, deceit or false statement was employed in obtaining the certificate, PIC or permit (RA 9292 §23); reinstatement of a revoked certificate may be granted **two (2) years** after revocation, on application and for sufficient reasons, provided that no illegal practice of the profession or violation of the Act, its rules, codes or policies occurred during the revocation period (§24); and the ninth enumerated act of the penal provision, RA 9292 §35, is “any person who shall violate any provision of this Act or any rules, regulations, the Code of Ethics and the Code of Technical Standards of Practice promulgated under this Act”, punished by a fine of not less than ₱100,000 nor more than ₱1,000,000, or imprisonment of not less than six (6) months nor more than six (6) years, or both, in the discretion of the court. Where a registrant's conduct also constitutes a crime — illegal wiretapping, cloning, hacking, cracking, piracy, unauthorised electronic eavesdropping, or maintaining an unlicensed or unregistered communications system or device — the same §35 range applies to a holder of a certificate and PIC (§35).

traps: Answering that IECEP membership is optional for a registered ECE. RA 9292 §32 makes every PECE, ECE and ECT, upon registration with the Commission, **ipso facto** a member of the accredited professional organization, and failure to maintain good standing lists the professional as delinquent in the roster.

Saying the Professional Regulation Commission or the Board “writes” the Code of Ethics alone. RA 9292 §30 has the **Board adopt** the Code of Ethics and the Code of Technical Standards of Practice, which are **promulgated by the accredited professional organization**; RA 9292 §39 adds Commission approval, publication and a 15-day effectivity period.

Answering that an ethics complaint is filed with the courts or with the PRC Central Office directly. The Board has jurisdiction under RA 9292 §7 and RA 8981 §9(c); the PRC is the **appeal** level, on a 15-day appeal period from the Board's decision.

Treating a licence suspension as the maximum consequence. Beyond suspension or revocation under RA 9292 §23, the violation of the Code of Ethics is the ninth enumerated act of the penal provision, RA 9292 §35, carrying ₱100,000–₱1,000,000 or 6 months–6 years imprisonment, or both.

Confusing the 15-day appeal period with the 2-year reinstatement period. Fifteen days is the window to appeal a Board decision to the Commission; two years is the minimum wait before a revoked certificate and PIC may be reinstated under §24.

Forgetting the concrete signing rule when the question is about sealing a colleague's work. RA 9292 §35 makes it an offence for a PECE to sign, seal or otherwise sign plans prepared by or under the supervision of **another** PECE unless the document clearly indicates the part of the work actually performed by the former — a Code-of-Ethics question dressed as a penal question.

Answering that a corporation may be licensed to practise electronics engineering. RA 9292 §28 forbids registering or licensing any firm, company, partnership, association or corporation for the practice, and makes the individual members responsible for their own respective acts where registrants practise collectively.

Reading the advertising canon as “no advertising at all.” The restriction is on misleading, self-laudatory, undignified or improperly solicited work; truthful professional announcements of available services are permitted.
